client: Lately, I’ve been really struggling with self-doubt after getting a low grade on my final project. I worked so hard on it, and seeing that grade just made me feel like I’m not cut out for college. I keep questioning whether I’m smart enough or capable enough to succeed, and it’s been hard to focus on anything else. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help—I feel like I’m just stuck in this mindset.
therapist: It sounds like that grade hit you really hard, especially after putting in so much effort. Let’s explore what’s behind these thoughts—what does “not being cut out for college” mean to you? Sometimes, our minds can magnify setbacks, but they don’t define our potential.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels like “not being cut out for college” means I’m just not smart enough or good enough to keep up with everyone else. I see my classmates doing well and it makes me feel like I’m falling behind or failing. I know setbacks happen, but this one feels so personal—like it’s proof I don’t belong here. I’m not sure how to stop feeling this way.
therapist: It sounds like you’re comparing yourself to others a lot, and that’s adding to the weight of this setback. Let’s unpack that—what does “smart enough” or “good enough” look like to you? Sometimes, our expectations for ourselves can be harsher than the reality.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: To me, “smart enough” means I should be able to handle everything effortlessly, like I see some of my classmates doing. They seem to get good grades without stressing, and I feel like I’m constantly struggling just to keep up. But I guess I don’t know if that’s really true—maybe they’re struggling too and just hiding it better. It’s hard to shake the feeling that I’m not measuring up, though.
therapist: It sounds like you’re holding yourself to a really high standard—expecting yourself to handle things effortlessly, which can add a lot of pressure. What do you think it would mean if it’s true that your classmates are also struggling, even if it’s not obvious? Sometimes, acknowledging that everyone has challenges can help soften those harsh comparisons.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if they’re struggling too, it might mean I’m not as alone as I feel. But it’s still hard to accept that, because it feels like everyone else has it together except me. I don’t know how to stop comparing myself—it’s like I can’t help but focus on where I fall short. Even if everyone has challenges, mine still feel bigger or more real somehow.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to see that others might be struggling too, but it’s still hard to let go of that feeling of being the only one who’s “falling short.” What do you think keeps you focused on where you feel you’re falling short, even when you know others have challenges too? Sometimes, it’s helpful to explore what we gain—or fear losing—by holding onto those comparisons.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think focusing on where I fall short makes me feel like I’m being honest with myself—like I’m not sugarcoating things or pretending I’m better than I am. But honestly, it also feels exhausting. I guess part of me is scared that if I stop being so hard on myself, I’ll slack off or stop trying as hard. It’s like I need this pressure to keep going, even though it’s draining me.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to be honest with yourself and feeling drained by the pressure you’re putting on yourself. What do you think it would look like to balance holding yourself accountable without being so hard on yourself? Sometimes, letting go of that pressure can actually help us grow, rather than hold us back.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess balancing accountability and self-compassion sounds good in theory, but I’m not sure how to actually do it. It feels like if I’m not hard on myself, I’ll just stop caring or give up entirely. I’m worried I’ll lose my drive if I’m not constantly pushing myself to do better. How do I know where the line is between being kind to myself and letting myself off the hook?
therapist: It sounds like you’re worried that self-compassion might lead to complacency, which is a really common concern. What do you think it would look like to hold yourself accountable while also giving yourself the kindness and understanding you’d offer a close friend? Sometimes, finding that balance starts with small shifts in how we talk to ourselves.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if I were talking to a friend, I’d tell them it’s okay to struggle and that one grade doesn’t define them. But when it comes to myself, it feels different—like I’m supposed to be tougher or stricter with myself. I’m not sure how to shift that mindset, though. It’s like I’ve been wired to think self-criticism is the only way to stay motivated. How do I even start changing that?
therapist: It’s striking how differently you’d treat a friend compared to yourself—almost like you hold yourself to a higher, harsher standard. What do you think it would feel like to start giving yourself even a fraction of the kindness you’d offer a friend? Small steps, like noticing when you’re being self-critical, can be a powerful place to begin.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It’s hard to imagine treating myself with that kind of kindness—it feels almost unnatural, like I’m letting myself off the hook too easily. But I guess it would feel less exhausting than constantly criticizing myself. I’m just not sure how to make that shift without feeling like I’m giving up or losing my edge. It’s like I’m stuck between wanting to be kinder to myself and fearing that kindness will make me complacent.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real tension here—wanting to be kinder to yourself but fearing it might lead to complacency. What do you think it would look like to experiment with small acts of self-kindness, just to see how it feels, without expecting it to change everything at once? Sometimes, testing the waters can help us find a balance that feels both supportive and motivating.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think experimenting with small acts of self-kindness could be worth a try, but I’m worried it won’t feel genuine. Like, if I try to be kind to myself, it might just feel forced or fake. I’m also not sure what those small acts would even look like—it’s hard to imagine what would feel meaningful without feeling like I’m just pretending.
therapist: It sounds like you’re open to trying but worried it might not feel authentic—that’s completely understandable. What do you think would make it feel more genuine for you? Even something small, like acknowledging your effort or giving yourself permission to take a break, might be a good place to start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think acknowledging my effort might feel more genuine than just telling myself everything’s okay—because it’s true, I did work hard on that project, even if the grade didn’t reflect it. But giving myself permission to take a break feels harder—like I’ll just be wasting time or falling further behind. I’m worried that if I ease up, I’ll lose my momentum completely.
therapist: It sounds like you’re comfortable acknowledging your effort, but the idea of taking a break brings up worries about losing momentum—almost like you’re afraid to pause because you might not start again. What do you think it would look like to test that belief? Maybe a short break could actually renew your energy rather than derail you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
